messages.author: 3bda7f3f64200ba0
messages.subject: left-truncation or bigger bin widths?
parts:
Hi,

I have surveyed roe deer along line transects in UK plantation forests
at night using a thermal imager. Logistically, I was constrained to
using tracks and roads as transects and so was unsurprised to find a
trough in my data at 0 distance. Observations of deer behaviour during
the surveys suggest that this was due to road avoidance as opposed to
movement in reaction to the observer. To cope with this at the analysis
stage, which is the most approporiate method: left truncation or
increased cut-offs? I have tried both and they yield different results:
left-truncation yields a higher density estimate with a fairly low CV
whereas increasing either the first cut-off only or all cut-offs yields
a lower density estimate with higher CVs. I have my opinion of which is
most appropriate but a referee of a recently submitted paper has a
different one!

With thanks,

Alastair

messages.author: f7f659b29e2c2571
messages.subject: Re: left-truncation or bigger bin widths?
parts:
Alastair,
I would like to hear both Dr. Thomas' and Buckland's
response to this
question, but in my experience, there is no justification
for left
truncation in the case where prior movement before detection
is not the
issue. I have seen this roadside avoidance in many parks I
have surveyed
for deer density. In my mind, this represents true density
variation driven
by animal behavior. Left truncation unnecessarily decreases
ESW and thus
inflates estimated density. I prefer fitting a hazard rate
function through
the hole out to the point where the observations "behave" as
they should
near the centerline. This analytical treatment seems to
work well in places
where I had mark-resight estimates of abundance for
comparison.

H. Brian Underwood
USGS Patuxent Wildlife Research Center
SUNY- College of Environmental Science & Forestry
Syracuse, NY 13210

messages.author: 4b4a7b00c1dd09c7
messages.subject: Re: left-truncation or bigger bin widths?
parts:
Hi Alastair,

I'm appending a reply to your message that was sent to me by one of our graduate
students, Tiago Marques. He's is currently at home in Portugal and can't post
directly to the list.

I'll add a bit to what he wrote:

The fundamental problem is that by surveying along roads you have violated two
important assumptions of the method:
- (a) animals are uniformly distributed with respect to distance from the
transect line. This allows us to interpret variation in numbers detected at
different distances as changes in detectability.
- (b) the density of animals in the surveyed region is representative of the
survey area. This allows us to extrapolate from the surveyed region to the
survey area.

Given this, it's going to be hard to get an unambiguous answer to your question.
I'm sure you've thought of this, but I wonder if there's an alternative way of
surveying the animals that would allow you to place the transects at random (or
systematic random, etc), for example dung surveys.

Anyway, the best mitigation step you could take will depend on the true
distribution of animals.

1. If the true distribution of animals shows a trough on the road but is then
more-or-less uniform after some distance, d, into the forest, and if the
probability of detection is still 1 at distance d, then moving the transect line
to distance d as Tiago suggests (below) and discarding all data <d will give an
estimate of the density of deer at distance > d from roads in the forest. If
density of deer at distance <d is effectively 0, then the estimated abundance in
the area >d from roads in the forest will also be the estimated abundance in the
whole forest (you'll need a GIS to work out how much forest is at distance >d
from roads).

2. It may be that deer are attracted to the road margin habitat, so that the
true density of deer has a trough on the road, a peak at the road margin, and is
then flat as you go farther into the forest. If you took the average of the
road and road margin, the density may be about the same as for the rest of the
forest. Sounds like a fantasy I know, but it may be about right. In this case,
the analysis is rather like an evasive movement analysis: you can combine the
data from the trough region and the peak region into one distance bin and then
use arbitrary bins after that to get an unbiased estimate of density. The
alternative is not to use bins at all, but to fit a detection function that is
flat though this region (using constraints and not too many adjustment terms).

As an aside, I'm not surprised that you got higher density after left truncation
-- you're now using a higher density patch of habitat. Nor am I surprised the
CV was less then -- the CV is generally higher when you bin data, especially if
you have few bins, and also the true density would be more uniform after
truncation so maybe a simpler detection function model may have been fit. What
Tiago says about sources of variation also applies though.

Hope this helps,

- Len

Hi Alastair

The data you describe are insuficent in order to answer your question,
nonetheless I would say that if any of the two methods will work is left
truncation (but only if an unlikely combination of events also occurs - see
below).

The fact is that your animals avoid the road, therefore, increasing the bin
width should not be an option, as even if you increase it enough to reach the
"peak" on your data, you will have far less animals on your first bin than you
would have if animals were not responsive to the road, therefore leading to an
underestimation of density. Note that as your using grouped data, Buckland et
al. 2001 (pag. 261) recomend that there should be at least two intervals in the
region of the shoulder of the detection function.

There are two possible aproachs to left truncation, a pure displacement of the
line or a left truncation where the detection function is extrapolated back to
the line. The second option makes no sense in your case, as you know there are
no animals (or much less) in the truncated area. The first left truncation
approach is dificult to implement, because in order to use standard distance
sampling methods, you have to assume that you left truncate at a poit where
detection probability is 1, otherwise if that probability is p, you
underestimate your density by a factor of p, in the sense that
trueD=estimatedD/p. If you can assume that you detect all the animals atthe
distance you left truncate, it might work.

Therefore, your results make sense, as you have a higher estimate using the left
truncation, and a lower estimate (probably using models constrained to be
monotonicaly decreasing) using large bins. Nonetheless, it's dificult to say
whether the larger estimate it's not an underestimation any way, which would
occur if not all animals at the distance to which your left truncating are
detected.

I am probably missing something, but I would expect the larger estimate to have
the larger CV, especially being the one where there is no left truncation,
therefore the one with more data. But it's dificult to tell without knowing if
the variance is dominated by encounter rate or f(0) variances. It may also be
the case that due to higher bin width you have much less bins, which would also
increase f(0)'s variance.

Hope it helps
Tiago
